claim: The hyperdirect pathway performs fast action cancellation.
source: The architecture of corticobasal ganglia pathways allows for many routes to inhibit a planned action: the hyperdirect pathway performs fast action cancellation and the indirect pathway competitively constrains execution signals from the direct pathway.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the hyperdirect pathway's function.

claim: The indirect pathway competitively constrains execution signals from the direct pathway.
source: The architecture of corticobasal ganglia pathways allows for many routes to inhibit a planned action: the hyperdirect pathway performs fast action cancellation and the indirect pathway competitively constrains execution signals from the direct pathway.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the indirect pathway's function.

claim: Reactive braking depends on the state of an execution process.
source: Using a nested diffusion model, we show how reactive braking depends on the state of an execution process.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by model fitting results.

claim: No-go decisions are best captured by a failure of the execution process to reach the decision threshold due to increasing constraints on the drift rate.
source: In contrast, no-go decisions are best captured by a failure of the execution process to reach the decision threshold due to increasing constraints on the drift rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by model fitting results showing drift modulation provides the best fit.

claim: The dependent process model accounts for both behavioral and fMRI responses during inhibitory control tasks better than alternative models.
source: This model accounts for both behavioral and functional MRI (fMRI) responses during inhibitory control tasks better than alternative models.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by AIC/BIC comparisons and fMRI data analysis.

claim: Proactive suppression is a slower, action-specific process.
source: These are generally considered to be separable control signals, with proactive suppression being a slower, action-specific process (Aron et al., 2011) and reactive inhibition being a fast global suppression mechanism (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Aron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reactive inhibition is a fast global suppression mechanism.
source: These are generally considered to be separable control signals, with proactive suppression being a slower, action-specific process (Aron et al., 2011) and reactive inhibition being a fast global suppression mechanism (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Aron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proactive signals modulate the efficacy of reactive stopping.
source: Indeed, recent evidence suggests that these processes interact, with proactive signals modulating the efficacy of reactive stopping (Aron, 2011; Chen et al., 2010; Forstmann et al., 2008; Irlbacher et al., 2014; Jahfari et al., 2012; Stuphorn and Emeric, 2012; van Belle et al., 2014; van Maanen et al., 2015; Zandbelt et al., 2013; Zandbelt and Vink, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Proactive signals have been most commonly associated with activity in rostral prefrontal and striatal areas.
source: Proactive signals have been most commonly associated with activity in rostral prefrontal and striatal areas (Cai et al., 2011; Majid et al., 2013; van Belle et al., 2014), suggesting a possible competition of facilitation and suppression signals relegated through the direct and indirect pathways, respectively (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Reactive braking has been linked to premotor and prefrontal areas in the right hemisphere, as well as the subthalamic nucleus, that together compose the hyperdirect pathway.
source: In contrast, reactive braking has been linked to premotor and prefrontal areas in the right hemisphere, as well as the subthalamic nucleus, that together compose the hyperdirect pathway (Aron et al., 2014; Cavanagh et al., 2011b; Rodriguez et al., 2006; Swann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies.

claim: The control signals of the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways all project to the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) in primates.
source: While in primates the control signals of the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways all project to the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), the primary output of the basal ganglia, it remains unclear whether these signals converge on the same pool of neurons or run in parallel of each other.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge about basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: It remains unclear whether the signals from direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways converge on the same pool of neurons or run in parallel of each other at the GPi.
source: While in primates the control signals of the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways all project to the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), the primary output of the basal ganglia, it remains unclear whether these signals converge on the same pool of neurons or run in parallel of each other.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: Successful reactive inhibition depends on the relative timing of descending execution signals from the striatum and fast-braking signals from the hyperdirect pathway at the output of the basal ganglia.
source: At the cellular level, successful reactive inhibition depends on the relative timing of descending execution signals from the striatum and fast-braking signals from the hyperdirect pathway at the output of the basal ganglia (Schmidt et al., 2013), suggesting that these two forms of control may, in fact, converge before they continue on to the thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological evidence.

claim: Changing the feedback structure promoted more cautious responding, resulting in more successful stopping at later stop signal delays.
source: As expected, in both conditions it was harder for participants to withhold their responses when the stop signal was delivered later in the trial (Figure 2B). In addition, changing the structure of the feedback promoted more cautious responding, resulting in more successful stopping at later stop signal delays (SSDs) and slower RTs on go trials.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Changing the feedback structure resulted in slower RTs on go trials.
source: In addition, changing the structure of the feedback promoted more cautious responding, resulting in more successful stopping at later stop signal delays (SSDs) and slower RTs on go trials.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The dependent process model provided a better fit to both the correct and incorrect RT distributions than either the interactive or independent race models.
source: The DPM provided a better fit to both the correct and incorrect RT distributions (Figure 3A) than either the interactive or independent race models.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dependent process model fell within the 95% confidence interval of the mean probability of stopping in each SSD condition, whereas the independent and interactive race models overpredicted the probability of stopping at the longest and shortest delays, respectively.
source: In addition, the DPM fell within the 95% confidence interval of the mean probability of stopping in each SSD condition (Figure 3B), whereas the independent and interactive race models overpredicted the probability of stopping at the longest and shortest delays, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The dependent process model was a substantially better fit to the data than the independent and interactive race models based on AIC and BIC.
source: Goodness of fit, assessed using both the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC), showed that the DPM was a substantially better fit to the data than the other two models (Figure 3C; Table 1), suggesting that the race between braking and execution signals may be biased depending on the state of the action selection decision.
evidence: This is supported by AIC and BIC values shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: The race between braking and execution signals may be biased depending on the state of the action selection decision.
source: Goodness of fit, assessed using both the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC), showed that the DPM was a substantially better fit to the data than the other two models (Figure 3C; Table 1), suggesting that the race between braking and execution signals may be biased depending on the state of the action selection decision.
evidence: This is inferred from the superior fit of the dependent process model.

claim: In the caution condition subjects shifted their stop curve later in time, producing more accurate stopping performance.
source: Overall, in the caution condition subjects shifted their stop curve later in time, producing more accurate stopping performance (Figure 2B; t (59) = −2.18, p=0.03) by delaying their execution decision, resulting in longer go trial RTs (Figure 2C t(59) =  −0.53, p <0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The drift modulation model provided the best overall fit of speed and accuracy in the reactive task.
source: As a result, the drift modulation model provided the best overall fit of speed and accuracy in the reactive task, followed by the onset modulation and boundary models, respectively (Figure 4; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by AIC and BIC comparisons shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Participants were able to use the colored cue to make accurate go and no-go decisions in the proactive task.
source: Participants were able to use the colored cue to make accurate go and no-go decisions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The probability of making a no-go decision scaled monotonically with the cued probability of a go trial.
source: There was a slight bias toward making a go decision across trial types; however, the probability of making a no-go decision scaled monotonically with the cued probability of a go trial.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Participants were faster with higher certainty of a go trial in the proactive task.
source: Also, as expected, participants were faster with higher certainty of a go trial (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All RTs in the proactive task were much faster than the responses in the reactive task.
source: It is worth noting that all RTs in this proactive task were much faster than the responses in the reactive task (Figure 2), confirming that subjects weren't relying on the delayed stop signal to make a reactive decision.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RT data between Figure 2 and Figure 5.

claim: There was no significant influence of demands for control on the decision curve in the proactive task.
source: Unlike the reactive task, we did not observe a significant influence of demands for control on either the decision curve (F[3.43, 205.8] = 0.76, p=0.53) or response times (F[2.28,132.32] = 0.81, p=0.46) in the proactive task.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a small but significant correlation between a subject's reactive stopping ability and their proactive decisions (r = 0.35, p <0.006, r2 = 0.06).
source: Collapsing across both the baseline and caution conditions, we found a small but significant correlation in a subject's reactive control abilities and their proactive decisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, r = 0.35, p <0.006, r2 = 0.06).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overall reactive task performance explains approximately 6% of the variance in the proactive condition.
source: Thus, overall reactive task performance explains ∼6% of the variance in the proactive condition, which is consistent with a model where these two abilities reflect separable upstream control signals that eventually converge on common output pathways (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is calculated from the r-squared value of the correlation analysis.

claim: The drift modulation model was able to capture the proactive no-go decision dynamics significantly better than the other models based on the AIC and BIC scores.
source: We found that the drift modulation model was able to capture the proactive no-go decision dynamics significantly better than the other models based on the AIC and BIC scores (Figure 6; Table 2) and general patterns of speed and response proportions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by AIC and BIC comparisons shown in Figure 6 and Table 2.

claim: As the go trial probability decreased, the drift rate of the execution process decreased to the point that the decision boundary was often not intersected by the end of the trial.
source: This means that as the go trial probability decreased, the drift rate of the execution process decreased to the point that the decision boundary was often not intersected by the end of the trial.
evidence: This is inferred from the best-fitting drift modulation model parameters.

claim: Activity in the right caudate nucleus and the left and right thalamic ROIs show a main effect of decision type on evoked activity.
source: Consistent with our predictions, activity in the right caudate nucleus and the left and right thalamic ROIs show a main effect of decision type on evoked activity (Figure 8; caudate: F(1,32) = 2.69, p=0.03; left thalamus: F(1,32) = 4.01, p=0.003; right thalamus: F(1,32) = 4.50, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the thalamus ROI responses selectively scaled with go trial probability, even in the trials where no key press was detected.
source: In the thalamus ROI responses selectively scaled with go trial probability, even in the trials where no key press was detected (Figure 8; left: F(2,32) = 4.13, p=0.025; right: F(3,32) = 3.67, p=0.037), while this effect was not significant in the caudate ROI (F2, 32] = 1.77, p=0.19).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The interaction between go trial probability and decision type was significant for both thalamus ROIs but not the caudate.
source: More importantly the interaction between go trial probability and decision type was significant for both thalamus ROIs (left: F[2,32] = 4.30, p=0.022; right: F[2,32] = 4.13, p=0.025), but not the caudate (F[2,32] = 1.22, p=0.31).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In the IFG, there was a lateralized interaction between go trial probability and response type in the right hemisphere but not in the left.
source: In the IFG, we observed a lateralized interaction between go trial probability and response type in the right hemisphere (F[2,38] = 4.05, p=0.027), but not in the left (F[2,38] = 1.45, p=0.25).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The SMA exhibited an interaction between go trial probability and response type in both the right and left hemispheres.
source: The SMA also exhibited an interaction between go trial probability and response type in both the right (F[2,38] = 4.86, p=0.014) and left (F[2,38] = 4.52, p=0.019) hemispheres.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: A dependent process model, where the initial state of the action cancellation signal depends on the current state of the execution decision, provides a much better fit to reactive stopping performance than models where these two processes are independent.
source: First, a DPM, where the initial state of the action cancellation signal depends on the current state of the execution decision, provides a much better fit to reactive stopping performance than models where these two processes are independent.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by model comparison results.

claim: The dependency between execution and braking processes is largely consistent with the circuit-level architecture of corticobasal ganglia pathways where the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways converge at the primary output nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: This dependency is largely consistent with the circuit-level architecture of corticobasal ganglia pathways (Figure 1A; Utter and Basso, 2008) where the direct (facilitation), indirect (suppression), and hyperdirect (brake) pathways converge at the primary output nucleus of the basal ganglia (i.e., the GPi in primates).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical literature and comparison with the model architecture.

claim: The dependent process model better fits behavioral data in the reactive task than the interactive race model.
source: Here we show, for the first time, that this dependency better fits behavioral data in the reactive task than the interactive race model, suggesting that there may not be equivalent control dynamics between oculomotor and manual response decisions.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results.

claim: There may not be equivalent control dynamics between oculomotor and manual response decisions.
source: Here we show, for the first time, that this dependency better fits behavioral data in the reactive task than the interactive race model, suggesting that there may not be equivalent control dynamics between oculomotor and manual response decisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in model fits between the current study and previous oculomotor studies.

claim: In rodents, an external stop cue reliably produces a burst of activity in the STN, but only results in a successful stop when this signal reaches the substantia nigra pars reticulata.
source: Schmidt et al. (2013) found that, in rodents, an external stop cue reliably produces a burst of activity in the STN, but only results in a successful stop when this signal reaches the substantia nigra pars reticulata (similar to the GPi in primates).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological evidence.

claim: Early activity of movement encoding striatal neurons was sufficient to predict whether hyperdirect stop signaling would reach the substantia nigra pars reticulata in time to prevent a response.
source: Consistent with classic race models of action cancellation, early activity of movement encoding striatal neurons was sufficient to predict whether hyperdirect stop signaling would reach the substantia nigra pars reticulata in time to prevent a response, rising rapidly on fast go and failed stop trials and more gradually on slow go and successful stop trials.
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological evidence from Schmidt et al. (2013).

claim: Parts of the action cancellation signal from the STN may be relegated via arkypallidal pathways that relay inhibitory signals back up to the striatal neurons.
source: Parts of this action cancellation signal from the STN may also be relegated via arkypallidal pathways (orange pathways in Figure 1A) that relay inhibitory signals back up to the striatal neurons, offering a route for hyperdirect signals to terminate action plans within the striatum itself (Dodson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical evidence.

claim: Cortical inputs to the striatum dynamically control the balance of direct and indirect signals throughout the basal ganglia.
source: Our framing of the execution process as a dynamic competition between direct and indirect pathways is motivated by the architecture of corticobasal ganglia pathways (Figure 1A), as well as recent electrophysiological and modeling evidence showing that cortical inputs to the striatum dynamically control the balance of direct and indirect signals throughout the basal ganglia (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological and modeling evidence.

claim: Proactive inhibition has been associated with hemodynamic responses in the dorsal striatum, interpreted as an increased recruitment of the indirect pathway to suppress an action.
source: For example, proactive inhibition has been associated with hemodynamic responses in the dorsal striatum (Majid et al., 2013), interpreted as an increased recruitment of the indirect pathway to suppress an action.
evidence: This is supported by citation to neuroimaging evidence.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in rodents find concurrent activation of both the direct and indirect pathways during action initiation and cancellation.
source: Yet, electrophysiological recordings in rodents find concurrent activation of both the direct and indirect pathways during action initiation and cancellation (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological evidence.

claim: Previous studies have largely found that proactive control is implemented as a change in the distance to threshold.
source: Previous studies have largely found that proactive control is implemented as a change in the distance to threshold (Cavanagh et al., 2011b; Forstmann et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2015; Jahfari et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2015); whereas in our model, these dynamics are captured by the rate of the execution process itself.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Slowing the rate of the execution process leads to greater stopping accuracy at the expense of response speed.
source: Rather, slowing the rate of the execution process leads to greater stopping accuracy at the expense of response speed.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the dependent process model.

claim: Ratcliff and Frank (2012) found that synthetic behavioral data generated by a basal ganglia neural network were best described by a drift-diffusion model with a decision threshold that collapsed at a rate that depended on the conflict between choices.
source: Also, Ratcliff and Frank (2012) found that synthetic behavioral data generated by a basal ganglia neural network were best described by a drift-diffusion model with a decision threshold that collapsed at a rate that depended on the conflict between choices.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Models that assume a temporal decay in the threshold or a nonconstant rate of accumulation predict response times that are more normally distributed compared with stationary diffusion models.
source: Compared with stationary diffusion models,  which predict positively skewed RT distributions, models that assume a temporal decay in the threshold or a nonconstant rate of accumulation predict response times that are more normally distributed (Hawkins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to modeling literature.

claim: Both tasks produced RT distributions that appeared more normal in shape and lacked a positive skew.
source: Indeed, both tasks produced RT distributions that appeared more normal in shape and lacked a positive skew, adding justification to the assumption of a dynamic bias in the execution process.
evidence: This is supported by observation of RT distributions in the data.

claim: Best-fit parameter estimates show a much stronger influence of the dynamic bias signal on 'go' decisions in the proactive than reactive task.
source: Correspondingly, best-fit parameter estimates show a muc stronger influence of the dynamic bias signal on 'go' decisions in the proactive than reactive task, suggesting that gain adaptation is differentially recruited during these two forms of inhibitory control.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of parameter estimates between tasks.

claim: Gain adaptation is differentially recruited during proactive and reactive forms of inhibitory control.
source: Correspondingly, best-fit parameter estimates show a muc stronger influence of the dynamic bias signal on 'go' decisions in the proactive than reactive task, suggesting that gain adaptation is differentially recruited during these two forms of inhibitory control.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in dynamic bias parameter estimates between tasks.

claim: Other models of behavioral and electrophysiological data in countermanding tasks have suggested that proactive constraints shift the onset of the decision process.
source: Other models of behavioral and electrophysiological data in countermanding tasks,  such as the anti-saccade task, have suggested that proactive constraints shift the onset of the decision process. This is particularly true in cortical neurons that plan the action (Pouget et al., 2011; Purcell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling and electrophysiological studies.

claim: The dynamics described in the current model may be the mechanism for the delayed onset of activity in downstream cortical motor areas.
source: Thus, it is possible that the dynamics described here are the mechanism for the delayed onset of activity in downstream cortical motor areas, that is, the onset of action selection neurons happens when the decision processes from the basal ganglia reach their boundary, which becomes delayed as the rate of the execution process is decelerated by the indirect pathway.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible reconciliation between the current model and previous findings.

claim: Subjects do not rely on a single mechanism for incorporating context into the decision process.
source: It is also well established by now that subjects do not rely on a single mechanism for incorporating context into the decision process (Heitz and Schall, 2012; Standage et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Some subjects may alternate between strategies of modulating the drift and onset across trials or use both simultaneously.
source: While the pattern of observed BOLD responses was generally consistent with the drift modulation predictions, it did share some characteristics with the predictions of the onset modulation model (i.e., increasing activity with go trial probability on 'no-go' trials and greater overall activation on 'go' trials), allowing for the possibility that some subjects may alternate between strategies of modulating the drift and onset across trials or use both simultaneously.
evidence: This is speculated based on mixed characteristics in the BOLD data.

claim: Reactive stopping ability depends on the competitive dynamics of ongoing proactive decision processes.
source: Taken together, our results provide crucial evidence that reactive stopping ability depends on the competitive dynamics of ongoing proactive decision processes, suggesting these two forms of control arise from convergent, but separable control signals in the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined behavioral and modeling results.

claim: Proactive and reactive control arise from convergent, but separable control signals in the basal ganglia.
source: Taken together, our results provide crucial evidence that reactive stopping ability depends on the competitive dynamics of ongoing proactive decision processes, suggesting these two forms of control arise from convergent, but separable control signals in the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined behavioral and modeling results.

claim: Neurologically healthy adults (N=60, mean age=22 years, 28 male) were recruited for the behavioral study.
source: Neurologically healthy adults (behavioral study: N=60, mean age=22 years, 28 male; imaging study: N=20, mean age=25 years, 9 male) were recruited from the local university population.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Neurologically healthy adults (N=20, mean age=25 years, 9 male) were recruited for the imaging study.
source: Neurologically healthy adults (behavioral study: N=60, mean age=22 years, 28 male; imaging study: N=20, mean age=25 years, 9 male) were recruited from the local university population.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All procedures were approved by the local institutional review board at Carnegie Mellon University.
source: All procedures were approved by the local institutional review board at Carnegie Mellon University.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The bar would intersect the target line 500 ms after trial onset in the go trials.
source: On each trial, participants would see a bar fill upwards toward a white target line on the screen. The bar would intersect the target line 500 ms after trial onset.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: In the reactive experiment, stop trials comprised 45% of trials.
source: In a subset of trials (stop trials; 45% trials), the bar would stop before it intersected with the target (i.e., the stop signal) and participants were instructed to not make a response on these trials.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: SSDs in the reactive experiment ranged from 200 to 400 ms.
source: SSDs ranged from 200 to 400 ms (n=20 trials per SSD).
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: In the proactive experiment, only one SSD was used at 450 ms.
source: In the proactive experiment, only one SSD was used (450 ms) for the entire experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the task description.

claim: All imaging data were collected in a 3T Siemens Verio MRI at the Scientific Imaging and Brain Research Center on the Carnegie Mellon University campus.
source: All imaging data were collected in a 3T Siemens Verio MRI at the Scientific Imaging and Brain Research Center on the Carnegie Mellon University campus.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Suprathreshold muscle activity was only observed in <1% (mean = 0.71%, max 4%) of the trials where no key press was detected in subjects with viable EMG data.
source: Viable EMG data was available for 14 subjects and in these subjects suprathreshold muscle activity was only observed in <1% (mean = 0.71%, max 4%) of the trials where no key press was detected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing EMG validation.

claim: After adjusting for cluster size (k > 40) and multiple comparisons (q < 0.05), 24 clusters were identified with differential modulation during no-go responses than go responses.
source: After adjusting for cluster size (k  > 40) and multiple comparisons (q  < 0.05) we identified 24 clusters with differential modulation during no-go responses than go responses (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the fMRI results section.
